name: toml++
baseline: toml11 v4.2.0 (also cpptoml, tomlc99 in the same matrix)
workload: Parse of nine generated TOML corpus files (0.25-1.5 MB each: array_heavy, cargo_like, datetime_heavy, deep_tables, mixed, scalar_float, scalar_int, scalar_string, table_heavy) from memory, min of 10 runs after 1 warmup, toml++ v3.4.0 vs toml11 v4.2.0.
claimed_speedup: Parse time in ms, toml++ vs toml11: array_heavy 12.0 vs 5168.8, cargo_like 7.3 vs 649.2, datetime_heavy 26.8 vs 584.9, deep_tables 5.4 vs 548.1, mixed 10.1 vs 503.3, scalar_float 65.2 vs 1159.3, scalar_int 37.1 vs 1156.1, scalar_string 25.2 vs 452.0, table_heavy 29.3 vs 2377.3; about 18x to 430x faster than toml11 across the nine shapes (derived from page data). Second data point: toml11 PR #320 (Intel i5-12600KF, 122-line config, 10000 parses) lists toml++ at 1178.6 ms and 1015.5 ms against 17850.4 ms and 18118.0 ms for toml11 before the PR (about 15x and 18x, derived from page data) and 4482.6 ms and 4859.9 ms after it (about 3.8x and 4.8x).
compiler_and_flags: Release build with -O3 -DNDEBUG -flto=thin via CMake (benchmarks/CMakeLists.txt, scripts/run_benchmarks.sh in leptris/teptris); compiler binary not named (thin LTO implies clang, macOS host); both toml++ and toml11 consumed as pinned single headers compiled into the same bench_parse binary.
tradeoffs: Header-only C++17 (optional compiled mode); parser does not preserve comments, whereas toml11 keeps comments and per-token error-location metadata, which accounts for part of the gap; supports serialising to TOML, JSON and YAML; works with or without exceptions and RTTI.
caveats: The win is against toml11 only. In the same matrix cpptoml (v0.5-era, TOML 0.5 semantics, rejects heterogeneous arrays) parses faster than toml++ on all 8 shapes it can parse (for example cargo_like 4.0 ms vs 7.3 ms, scalar_float 24.3 ms vs 65.2 ms), tomlc17 is faster on some shapes, and teptris (the benchmark author's own C library) is 3.2-7.5x faster than toml++. The benchmark was written by the author of a competing TOML parser (teptris) and published in its own repository, so it is independent of toml++ and toml11 but not a neutral suite; it falls short of tier A because the compiler is not named and the toml++ and toml11 numbers come from a single machine. toml11 is pinned at v4.2.0 and its 4.4.0 release notes claim parse is 2x faster, so the ratio is overstated against current toml11; toml11 per-token error metadata makes it a slow baseline (0.1-1.9 MB/s here). Run on generated corpora (seed 42), not real-world configs. toml++'s own repo has only examples/parse_benchmark.cpp (a timing loop, no comparison) and no published numbers; the PR #320 numbers come from an open third-party PR with no compiler or flags stated. Linux x86_64 gcc CI numbers exist in the same ledger but give no toml++ figures.
